name: Nasal saline rinse / neti pot

lead: Nasal irrigation rinses mucus and debris from the nose and sinuses using saline from a neti pot, squeeze bottle, bulb syringe or electric device. It has roots in Ayurvedic practice (jala neti), and appearance communities use it to clear congestion that they link to under-eye darkness and puffiness.

A saline stream flushes mucus, allergens and debris from the nasal passages. Reviews cited on Wikipedia report it can relieve acute sinusitis symptoms, may temporarily help allergic rhinitis, and has weak evidence in chronic sinusitis. Appearance effects were not examined.

paras: People rinse once or twice a day, often during allergy season or colds, using a premixed saline packet and a neti pot or squeeze bottle with safe water.

Side effects are generally mild: irritation, nosebleeds, headache. Rare fatal Naegleria fowleri infections followed neti-pot use with tap water, including two deaths in 2011, and the FDA warned in 2017 that improper use can be harmful. The CDC advises boiled, filtered (NSF 53/58 or 1 micron), sterile or distilled, or disinfected water.

web.title: Rinsing Your Sinuses with Neti Pots Safely - FDA

angle.text: Users rinse the nose with saline on the idea that clearer sinuses mean less congestion and pressure around the eyes, and so less congestion-related under-eye darkness. Studies cover symptom relief in sinusitis and allergic rhinitis, not appearance.

lead: Nasal irrigation, also called nasal lavage or, when done with the vessel known as a neti pot, jala neti, is a hygiene practice that flushes mucus, allergens and debris from the nose with a saline solution. It is traced to Ayurveda, where jala neti (water) and sutra neti (string) were part of personal hygiene and a yogic technique.[1] The FDA describes rinsing devices as a way to ease congestion from sinus problems, colds and allergies and to moisten dry nasal passages.[2]

In appearance-focused communities the rinse is discussed as a way to keep the nose clear and reduce allergy-related congestion, which proponents link to dark circles, facial puffiness and easier nasal breathing. Some also associate steady nasal breathing with facial posture and sleep quality. Published studies have measured symptom relief rather than looks, so these links remain proponents' reasoning.

Research summarised on Wikipedia and in guidelines indicates irrigation can relieve acute sinusitis symptoms from upper respiratory infections, may temporarily relieve allergic rhinitis symptoms, and has weaker support in chronic sinusitis.[1][3][4][5] It is generally well tolerated, with irritation, nosebleeds and headache reported.[1][5] Water safety is the main documented hazard: tap water has been linked to rare fatal amoebic infections, and the FDA and CDC publish guidance on which water to use.[1][2][6]
infobox: Neti pot, squeeze bottle, bulb syringe, electric irrigator[1]
Isotonic saline; some clinicians add budesonide[1]
Acute sinusitis symptoms, allergic rhinitis, post-sinus-surgery care[1][7]
FDA: distilled, sterile, or boiled-and-cooled water[2]
Amoebic infection from untreated tap water[1][16]

paras: Neti pots use gravity and head position: saline is poured into one nostril and drains from the other. Squeeze bottles apply the fluid by hand, bulb syringes are common for infants, and electric machines use pumps.[1] Otolaryngologists describe these methods and commercial sprays as options for sinonasal irrigation, and a 2023 review notes it is unclear whether electric devices have any advantage over simpler ones.[7]

Saline is the common solution. Some irrigations carry added medications such as the steroid budesonide, which clinicians use in chronic rhinosinusitis.[1] A 2009 paper on fluid residuals and drug exposure observed that additives like menthol add sensory feedback, while steroids and antibiotics are pharmaceutical agents about which little was known regarding how much fluid is retained and absorbed.[8]

The isotonic saline recipe described on Wikipedia uses about a quarter of a litre of tepid, sterilized drinking water with roughly half a level teaspoon of table salt.[1] Tap water is generally advised against unless it has been boiled and cooled.[1][2]

The CDC lists four water options: boiling for one minute (three minutes above 6,500 feet) then cooling; filtering with an NSF 53 or NSF 58 device or an absolute pore size of 1 micron or smaller; buying distilled or sterile water; or disinfecting with chlorine bleach at the correct level and time.[1] The FDA consumer guidance adds that devices should be washed and dried between uses and used per the manufacturer's directions.[2]

Wikipedia traces nasal rinsing to Indian Ayurveda, whose roots reach to the Vedas, where daily nasal cleansing formed part of personal hygiene (soucha). Jala neti is an old yogic technique, and sutra neti is a second method using a string instead of water.[1]

A 2016 study in Health Communication used discourse analysis of US popular press and new media to follow the neti pot's path. In about a decade it shifted from an obscure Ayurvedic device to mainstream complementary and integrative medicine, touted by celebrities and sold widely in drug stores; the authors treat it as a case study in how a foreign health practice becomes mainstream.[9] The same media attention carried safety stories: in 2011 two deaths were tied to neti pots filled with tap water.[1]

Modern squeeze bottles and electric irrigators carry the practice into allergy and sinus care, and irrigation after endoscopic sinus surgery is described in the otolaryngology literature as a routine adjunct.[7]

Proposed mechanisms listed on Wikipedia are soothing of inflamed tissue, removal of irritants such as allergens, and help clearing mucus.[1] A 2021 simulation study states that saline irrigation improves mucociliary transport and helps remove inflammatory mediators and post-surgical debris.[10]

Delivery research looks at where the fluid goes. A 2008 cadaver study using CT scans found sinus distribution was greater after sinus surgery and differed by device, with neti pot distributing more than squeeze bottle and squeeze bottle more than pressurised spray.[11] A 3D-printed model study found penetration is variable and depends on a person's anatomy and technique such as head position and flow rate.[12] Computational models of real airway geometry found that head position and inflow direction strongly influenced filling of the maxillary sinuses, while the choice of nostril made little difference to nasal cavity filling.[10][13]

The practice appears in appearance discussions as a way to reduce allergic congestion, which proponents link to dark circles and facial puffiness, and to keep the nose clear for easier nasal breathing. No published study has examined rinsing in relation to under-eye appearance or facial puffiness.
No studies found on appearance outcomes. Studies of symptoms are summarised below.

A 2015 clinical practice guideline update on adult sinusitis (Rosenfeld and colleagues) concluded that irrigation can relieve acute sinusitis symptoms from upper respiratory infections such as the common cold.[1][3]

A 2012 systematic review and meta-analysis by Hermelingmeier and colleagues pooled ten randomized trials with over 400 participants, including children and pregnant women, that tested saline irrigation in allergic rhinitis. Over periods of up to seven weeks, regular irrigation was associated with better symptom scores, quality of life and mucociliary clearance and with reduced medication use. The authors describe it as safe, inexpensive and easy, and also note that the trials were small and varied in method, solution and duration.[4]

A Cochrane review of saline irrigation for chronic rhinosinusitis (Chong and colleagues, 2016) described the supporting evidence as weak and reported adverse effects as generally mild, including irritation, nosebleeds, headache and drainage.[1][5]

Laboratory and modelling work examines delivery rather than outcomes, using cadaver, 3D-printed and computational airway models.[11][12][13][10] Early pandemic-era papers explored nasal lavage in COVID-19: one proposed using a jal neti sample for virus detection as a hypothesis, and a 2023 preprint described hypochlorous acid lavage and symptoms in ambulatory patients; neither concerns ordinary saline rinsing for looks.[14][15]
Common effects are mild: irritation, nosebleeds, headache and drainage after use.[1][5]

Tap water may contain microbes harmless to drink but dangerous in the nose. Naegleria fowleri infection occurs when contaminated water enters the nose and reaches the brain; Wikipedia states that swallowing it does not cause infection, and that nasal irrigation accounts for about 9 percent of known worldwide cases.[16] The CDC describes such infections as rare but almost always fatal and names tap water used for sinus rinsing as a route.[6] Wikipedia's nasal irrigation article records two deaths in 2011 tied to neti pots filled with tap water, a 2013 Louisiana death from the same amoeba, and a 2018 Balamuthia mandrillaris infection after a month of tap water filtered through a household purifier.[1]

The FDA stated on 24 January 2017 that improper use can be harmful.[1] Its consumer guidance says tap water is not safe for rinsing because amoebas and other organisms that are harmless when swallowed can survive in the nose, and advises distilled or sterile water, tap water boiled for several minutes and cooled, or water from a filter designed to trap infectious organisms. It advises consulting a clinician first for people with weakened immune systems and using the devices on children only on a pediatrician's advice.[2]

Case reports show that other infections have been reported with rinsing. A 2020 report describes Streptococcus pneumoniae meningitis in a man who rinsed several times a day with distilled water, and the authors ask clinicians to inquire about rinse use.[17] A 2018 conference abstract reports Acanthamoeba disease associated with nasal rinsing in immunocompromised patients.[18]

Pressurised saline sprays, medicated steroid irrigations after sinus surgery and the string-based sutra neti are related approaches described in the sources above.[1][11][7] Sutra neti is described by Wikipedia as a second Ayurvedic technique that uses a string instead of water.[1]

lore.intro: In appearance and wellness circles, nasal rinsing is described as a low-cost way to keep allergies and congestion from affecting how the face looks and how well the nose works. Claims go further than the published trials, which study symptoms.[1][9]

claims.claim: Rinsing reduces allergy congestion and the puffy, tired look that comes with it
A neti pot is a traditional, natural practice with long-standing benefits
Tap water is fine because it is safe to drink
The pricier the device, the better the rinse reaches the sinuses
Rinsing can also help flush out viruses

Cadaver CT study compares sinus distribution from neti pot, squeeze bottle and pressurised spray.[11]
